sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
None.

One point the checklist has no line for: the "Orders and shipping" card (943–1215, 580–746 px) says "Track a delivery or start a return." Every other card describes a team workspace tool: inviting your team, two-step sign-in, calendar and chat integrations, sync errors. A first-time viewer may wonder whether this help center covers a product they actually use, or whether the copy came from a template. This is a minor point, judged on common sense. The fix is to check that each topic belongs to this product, and to cut or reword any that don't.

**What's working.**
- **Clear purpose at a glance.** The page says what it is right away. The serif "How can we help?" sits centred over a search field on a navy band, and a labelled grid of topics follows below. A visitor knows within a second that they can search or pick a topic, so no explanation is needed (Krug, *Don't Make Me Think*).
- **Consistent cards.** All eight cards share one pattern: an outline icon, a bold title and a two-line grey description in the same box. The grid reads as one set of equal choices, so visitors compare topics by their words rather than by style. The serif headline is the only different typeface, and it marks the one entry point without breaking the calm navy-and-grey mood.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- **What's below the cards.** The capture ends about 50 px under the second row of cards. It doesn't show whether the page goes on to popular articles or a way to reach a person, which matters for visitors whose problem isn't one of the eight topics. Scroll the live page to check.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 8 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Below the first element, can you tell each level of the text (title, headings, body, captions) from the next at a glance, with no two sizes almost the same?** No.
   - **Where:** The section heading "Browse by topic" (about x64–204, y352–372) looks like about 18 px bold dark sans. The card titles just below it ("Getting started", "Account and sign-in" and so on, y477–495 and y665–683) look like about 16 px bold dark sans. Same face, same weight, same colour, a step or two apart in size. The "Harbor Help Center" logo (about 20 px bold, navy) is another near-neighbour at the top left.
   - **What the viewer experiences:** The heading doesn't read as the label over the grid. It reads as a ninth title that has fallen out of its card. The page has two levels that are meant to differ, section and item, but they look like one level, so the grid seems to start with no heading.
   - **Why:** Dair, *Design with Type*, ch. 8: a heading one size larger than its text "looks like an accident, not a choice". A difference only counts when it is obvious at a glance in size, weight, structure, form or colour. Bringhurst, *The Elements of Typographic Style*, 3.1.1: sizes should come from a modest set of distinct intervals.
   - **Direction of the fix:** Make "Browse by topic" plainly different from the card titles in at least one way. Options are a clear size step up, the H1's serif (which would also tie the page together), or a small grey or capitals label style. The other option is to drop it to a quiet label so the cards carry the level alone.
   - **Kind and weight:** Convention. Minor: the cards still group themselves by their borders, so finding a topic isn't slowed much.

**What's working.**
- "How can we help?" clearly dominates. It is the largest type on the page, the only serif, and white on the one dark band, so the eye starts there and drops straight to the search field. That entry point is right for a help center.
- Inside each card, the title and description differ in weight (bold against regular) and colour (near-black against grey), not only in size. The eight cards scan cleanly by title.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 2 yes, 1 no (text levels distinct, with no two sizes almost the same)

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. *Is every element either exactly aligned with an edge or axis it shares with another, or clearly off it, with no near-misses of a few pixels?* No. The search field (about x 360–920, y 216–264) is centred and nearly as wide as the two middle card columns below it (about x 357–922), but misses their outer edges by about 2–3 px on each side. Only a careful viewer will notice, because the edge of the navy band sits between the field and the cards. Still, it is the one spot where an edge that looks meant to line up doesn't quite, and it makes the hero look laid out separately from the grid. Mark it **convention**: near-misses read as errors (Müller-Brockmann, *Grid Systems in Graphic Design*, "Construction of the grid"; Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, ch. I "Balance"). Fix: make the field span exactly from the left edge of card column 2 to the right edge of column 3, or make it clearly narrower or wider than that span. Measure it in the live page to confirm the pixel offset. Weight: **minor**.

**What's working.**
- **One strict grid sets the page.** The logo, the "Browse by topic" heading and the first card column share the 64 px left edge. The nav and the last card column end together at about x 1216. Card gutters look like the same ~21 px across and down. The page reads as one system, and all eight topics look like equal choices. Keep this when topics are added: the grid should take more rows, not uneven card sizes.
- **Spacing makes the groups.** Inside each card, the bigger gap between icon and title and the tighter gap between title and description tie each title to its own description. The "Browse by topic" heading sits about 30 px above the cards and about 48 px below the edge of the hero, so it clearly belongs to the cards it introduces.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 12 yes, 1 no (exactly aligned or clearly off, with no near-misses), 0 unsure

I found one minor defect in the text section and none in the other 29 lines.

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do paragraphs and columns break cleanly, with no lone short word on a last line and no heading at the foot of a column?** In five of the eight topic cards (roughly y 512–532 in row 1 and y 700–720 in row 2), the two-line description ends in a single word alone on its second line:
   - "Passwords, two-step sign-in, and / recovery." (x≈380)
   - "Plans, payment methods, and / receipts." (x≈673)
   - "How we protect and store your / data." (x≈87, row 2)
   - "Choose which alerts you get and / where." (x≈673, row 2)
   - "Fix sync problems and error / messages." (x≈966, row 2)

   **What the viewer sees:** The text is small and the second lines are short, so they don't slow reading much. But the grid looks uneven: five cards end in a stub, two end in a fuller line, and "Orders and shipping" fits on one line. The cards look set by default rather than cared for. In "data." and "where." the word left alone is the one that finishes the meaning, so the line reads as cut off for a moment.

   **Why:** Bringhurst, *The Elements of Typographic Style*, section 2.4.2: a paragraph should not end with one short word alone on its last line.

   **Fix:** Balance the two lines so each blurb breaks at a phrase boundary, for example "How we protect / and store your data." or "Choose which alerts / you get and where." Line balancing (`text-wrap: balance` or `pretty`) does this automatically. You could also edit each blurb to one line or two full lines.

   **Type and weight:** Convention. Minor.

**What's working.**
- **Headline face:** The serif in "How can we help?" (centred, ~x 485–795, y 115–155) is the only serif on the page and is plainly different from the sans used everywhere else. That reads as a deliberate accent, not two faces fighting. It gives the entry point a warmer voice without competing with the plain, readable card text.
- **Card text:** Each card's text is set in clearly separate levels: a bold dark title over a lighter, regular-weight grey description, both flush left under the icon. Title and description differ by weight and colour, not just size, so you can scan the titles across the grid without reading the blurbs.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 29 yes, 1 no (paragraphs break cleanly, no lone last-line word).

sections.report:
Walk (working notes):

First read: the eye lands on the navy band and the white serif "How can we help?", drops to the white search field, then down to the grid of eight white cards on pale gray. It reads as a help center for a SaaS product. Calm, cool and quiet. Assumed job: help customers find a topic or search the help articles quickly.

Color:
- Small palette: yes. Navy (hero, logo, icons, headings), a slate gray for body text, white, and a pale blue-gray background.
- Strong color kept to a small share: yes. The navy band covers about a third of the height, but it is dark and muted, not saturated.
- Clear range of light and dark: yes. Dark band, light field and light cards would all hold up in grayscale.
- Warm forward, cool back: yes. Everything is cool, and nothing warm competes with the headline or search.
- Matching colors look the same: yes. The icon navy and heading navy look the same across all eight cards, and the white field and white cards look the same white.
- No vibrating edges: yes.
- Status colors used for their usual meaning: yes. There are none.
- Meaning not shown by color alone: yes. Nothing is coded by color.
- Dark theme background is dark gray: yes. It's a light theme, and the navy band is a dark blue-gray, not black.

No line came out `no` or `unsure`, so I didn't open any entries.

**Section.** Color: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **Light and dark carry the page's structure.** The single dark navy band (y 64–312) against the white header and the pale blue-gray body splits the page into "ask" and "browse" with no other help. The white search field (360–920, y 216–264) is the lightest thing sitting on the darkest area, so it's the strongest contrast on the page, and that's the right place for it on a help center. Keep that one dark band and don't add a second dark area that would compete with it.
- **The palette stays tight.** One navy carries the logo, the hero, the card titles and the line icons, with a slate gray for descriptions and nav. The whole page reads as one brand. Because no hue is spent on decoration, a later accent such as a link color or an alert would stand out right away. That's my view as a designer (taste).

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure.

**First read (working notes).** The eye lands on the serif "How can we help?" in the navy band, drops to the search field, then moves to the 4×2 grid of topic cards. Each card leads with a small navy line icon. This is a SaaS help-centre home page, meant for customers who want to find an answer quickly. It feels calm and orderly, but generic.

**Job (assumed).** This is a help-centre landing page that sends users to a topic or to search. The pictures here are the eight card icons and the "Harbor Help Center" text wordmark.

Bash was refused, so I worked from the whole 1280×800 image with no zoomed crops. At about one screen in size, the image did not need crops anyway.

**Walk: Pictures**
- Every image shows its content, with no broken images or placeholders: yes
- Full quality, sharp and unstretched: yes. The icons look crisp at this size.
- Crops look intended: yes. Every icon is whole.
- Subject stands apart from its background: yes. The navy strokes sit on white cards.
- One rendering style and one level of detail: yes. All eight are outline icons with no fill.
- Photos treated consistently: yes. There are no photos.
- Icons share one stroke weight, cap style and corner radius: yes. They look like one icon set. The key (≈386–414, 418–446) looks optically a little lighter and smaller than the rest. That is within normal variation, not a finding.
- Objects in a scene share one viewpoint and light: yes. There is no scene. The isometric box is a standard glyph for this kind of icon set.
- Texture or pattern stays quiet: yes. There is none.
- Surfaces look like what they are: yes. Flat cards with hairline borders.
- Logo has clear space, no distortion, its own colours: yes. The wordmark at top left (64–252, 20–44) has plenty of room.
- Logo is simple enough to read small and in one colour: yes. It is a single-colour text wordmark.

Every line is yes, so step 5 has no entries to open.

---

**Section.** Pictures: applies. The pictures are the eight topic-card line icons and the text wordmark.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **One icon family.** The eight icons are the same size (about 30 px), drawn with the same thin stroke, in the same navy, and each sits in the same top-left spot on its card (about 24 px in, 26 px down). Because they match, the grid reads as one system, and the eye scans the bold labels instead of comparing the drawings. Any new topic should use an icon from the same set at the same size.
- **Icons that match their topics.** The key is sign-in, the card is billing, the box is orders, the shield is privacy, the plug is integrations, the bell is notifications and the lifebuoy is troubleshooting. Each one confirms its label at a glance. The lightning bolt for "Getting started" is the loosest fit, but it is still a common choice for that topic.

**Checklist.** Pictures: 12 lines, 12 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

sections.report:
**Walk (working notes).** The image is 1280×800, about one screen, so no crops are needed. Bash is denied in this session, so I couldn't run the crop or entries scripts and worked from the whole image.

First read: the eye lands on "How can we help?", drops to the white search field on navy, then scans the 4×2 grid of topic cards. It reads as a SaaS help centre home page: calm and generic.

Interface:
1. One primary action: yes. There are no buttons, and search is plainly the main control.
2. Controls look like what they do: yes.
3. Non-text contrast at 3:1: yes. The card borders are faint, but the cards are identified by their titles, and the icons are dark navy.
4. States shown: yes. None are shown.
5. Focus indicator: unsure, can't tell from a still.
6. Focus not obscured: unsure, can't tell from a still.
7. Main content uncovered: yes.
8. Target size: yes.
9. Phone thumb zone: yes, this is a desktop layout.
10. Where the user is: yes. This is the home page, reached through the logo.
11. Way out: yes, there is no dialog.
12. Valid inputs: yes.
13. Destructive actions: yes, there are none.
14. Recognition over recall: yes.
15. Progressive disclosure: yes.
16. Visible field label: **no**. The search field has only placeholder text, with no magnifier icon and no submit button.
17. Natural mapping: yes.
18. One-column form: yes.
19. Required markers: yes, not applicable.
20–22. Errors and empty states: yes, not applicable.
23. Help near the step: yes.
24. Shortcuts: yes, search is offered.
25. Anticipation: yes.
26. Conventions: yes.
27. Audience's words: yes.
28. Link purpose: yes.
29. Sensory characteristics: yes.
30. Conceptual model: **no**. The hero says "search the guides", and "Guides" is also a separate nav item with no current marker, so the user can't tell whether they are already in Guides.
31. Consistency across screens: yes.
32. Reflow: yes.
33. Dark patterns: yes.

---

**Section.** Interface: applies. There is a header nav, a search field and eight topic cards that act as links.

**Findings**
1. **Does every field have its own visible label, closer to it than to any other field, not a placeholder alone?** No. The search field (about x 360–920, y 216–264) is labelled only by the placeholder "Search for articles". It has no magnifier icon and no submit button.
   - **What the viewer experiences:** While the field is empty it reads clearly as search. Once someone types, the placeholder disappears and nothing on the field says what it is or how to submit. A user who doesn't think to press Enter has no visible way to run the search. The line above it, "Browse a topic or search the guides.", is a sentence about two choices, not a label for the field.
   - **Why:** Placeholder text is not a label (NN/g, and WCAG 3.3.2 "Labels or instructions"). A single search box is the usual exception, but only when a magnifier icon or a search button marks it, and this field has neither.
   - **Fix:** Add a magnifier icon inside the field and a "Search" button, or an arrow button, at its right end. Also give the field a programmatic label.
   - **Kind:** convention. **Weight:** minor. Search is the main task on the page, but the placeholder still makes it legible at first glance.
2. **Do the grouping, names, and navigation show how the product's parts relate?** No. The hero offers to "search the guides", and the nav (about x 880–930, y 30) lists "Guides" as a separate destination. Nothing in the nav is marked as the current page.
   - **What the viewer experiences:** A user can't tell whether this page is the Guides section or something above it. Clicking "Guides" might bring them back to what they're already looking at, or to a different index that duplicates these eight topics.
   - **Why:** The catalog entry for this line is Norman, *The Design of Everyday Things*, "Conceptual model". I couldn't open the entry in this session, so this is my judgment that the case fits it, not a citation of the entry's own wording.
   - **Fix:** Pick one structure. Either this page is Guides, so mark "Guides" as current or drop it from the nav. Or Guides is a separate section, so change the hero copy so it doesn't use the same word for this page.
   - **Kind:** taste, argued on common sense. **Weight:** minor.

**What's working.**
- Search is the clear first action. The white field is the brightest shape on the dark band, sits right under the question, and is wide enough to show it takes free text. Someone arriving with a problem knows where to start in about a second.
- The topic cards are easy to click: each is a large target, and the bold titles sit above one-line descriptions that use the user's words ("Passwords, two-step sign-in, and recovery", "Track a delivery or start a return"). People can tell which card fits their problem without opening any of them.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- Focus indicators on the search field, nav links and cards. On a keyboard-driven help page, check that each control shows a visible ring at least 2 px thick with 3:1 contrast.
- Hover states on the cards. They are the main way people browse here, so check that they visibly respond.

**Checklist.** Interface: 33 lines, 29 yes, 2 no (every field has its own visible label; grouping, names, and navigation show how the product's parts relate), 2 unsure (focus indicator 2 px with 3:1 contrast; focused control not obscured).
